strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine misalignment between existing robustness evaluation (text-ignoring) and real-world LVLM requirements (joint object and text understanding)
Elegant benchmark design using same-scene counterfactuals that isolate selective text use by holding visual content constant while varying question type and attack condition
Comprehensive experimental validation across 6 models of varying scales with thorough ablations (Table 2 reveals language model's primary role in selective text use)
Rigorous construction pipeline with careful controls: hierarchical negative sampling, multi-level attack difficulty, distance-controlled placement avoiding text occlusion
Generalization studies on multiple datasets (Typo-D, AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, InfoVQA) demonstrating cross-domain transfer without degrading text-reading ability
Clear presentation with effective motivation (Figure 1), intuitive taxonomy (Figure 2), and extensive reproducible supplementary materials
Important insight that vision-centric defenses are inherently incompatible with LVLMs performing text reading, challenging prior work
weaknesses: Limited scope despite generality claims: instantiated only on TextVQA with 21,953 images; not extended to other dual-annotation datasets despite claiming this is straightforward
Attack realism concerns: simple synthetic text overlays may not fully capture sophisticated physical/adversarial typographic attacks (e.g., SceneTAP); no human evaluation of attack plausibility
Unfair baseline comparison: IT-RT trained on 8k samples vs. RIO-RT on 12k; equal sample budgets would provide cleaner comparison of balanced training efficacy

Limited novelty in defense method: RIO-RT is essentially balanced supervised finetuning without theoretical justification or explicit decision mechanism; lacks comparison to alternative approaches (multi-task learning, routing mechanisms)
Missing statistical significance testing and confidence intervals across experiments; unclear which performance differences are meaningful
Synthetic object-centric questions lack human validation for naturalness and diversity; template-based generation may introduce subtle biases
Incomplete analysis: no error case studies, limited investigation of semantic properties affecting attack effectiveness, insufficient ablations on design choices (7×7 grid, distance thresholds)
Generalization results are mixed with minor degradation on some text-centric datasets (Table 4); domain-specific nature of learned capability suggests narrow transfer
Metric design choices lack justification: R-CLIP-M weighting of correctness vs. attack resistance appears arbitrary; distance-based attack placement strategy (near/mid/far tertiles) is ad-hoc
Scope limitations acknowledged but significant: VQA-only evaluation, scene text focus, unclear extension to documents/charts; impact on real-world robustness scenarios remains unvalidated

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine gap in typographic robustness evaluation where existing work implicitly encourages text-ignoring while real applications require joint object-text reasoning.
Careful benchmark construction: Same-scene counterfactuals eliminate confounds; hierarchical attack generation with controlled difficulty; R-CLIP-M metric balancing correctness and robustness.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Consistent findings across 6 model architectures; clear evidence that strong LVLMs and existing defenses fail to balance robustness and text understanding; useful LoRA ablation showing selective text use learned via language model reasoning.
Reproducibility and clarity: Detailed construction pipeline, extensive supplementary materials, clear presentation of task design and counterfactual evaluation.
Practical benchmark value: RIO-Bench enables training-based defenses and provides structured evaluation foundation for future work.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: RIO-VQA task is essentially answering different question types correctly with question-type as an overly strong signal; RIO-RT is standard balanced supervised fine-tuning with no novel mechanism; benchmark construction applies existing techniques to combine TextVQA and Open Images.

Questionable task formulation realism: Same-scene counterfactuals are artificial—real scenarios don't present identical scenes requiring different read/ignore behavior based on question framing. Question type is an unrealistic proxy for determining selective text use; true real-world ambiguity about text relevance is not captured.

Insufficient experimental rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple random seeds reported; R-CLIP-M metric lacks human validation and theoretical justification; generalization results mixed (Table 4 shows degradation on external text-VQA datasets in some cases).

Shallow mechanistic analysis: Limited investigation of why models fail at selective text use; attention visualizations show shifts but provide minimal insight; no ablation on context types or investigation of alternative training approaches (e.g., auxiliary losses, explicit read/ignore tokens).

Attack realism concerns: Simple text overlays with fixed fonts/colors do not reflect sophisticated adversarial perturbations; no human evaluation of attack quality; distance-based placement strategy lacks justification.

Scope limitations acknowledged but significant: Restricted to VQA and natural scene text (~22k images); does not explore structured text (documents, charts) or other tasks (captioning, visual reasoning) mentioned as motivation; TextVQA foundation biases results toward specific patterns.

Limited baseline comparisons: Only one prior defense (CoT, 2024); no adaptation of vision-centric defenses; strawman IT-RT baseline (text-suppression only); missing comparison to other recent typographic robustness work.

Missing crucial analyses: No correlation between R-CLIP-M and human robustness judgments; no Pareto frontier analysis of robustness-accuracy trade-offs; insufficient investigation of generalization failures shown in Table 4.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: identifies the critical trade-off between typographic robustness and text-reading ability, revealing a fundamental misalignment in existing evaluation paradigms
Elegant benchmark design with same-scene counterfactuals: the orthogonal taxonomy (object vs. text questions × clean vs. attacked) enables controlled, confound-free evaluation within identical scenes
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 6 diverse LVLMs, multiple defense strategies, thorough ablations (attack levels, LoRA placement, data size), and generalization studies to external datasets

Technically sound construction pipeline: principled attack generation with hierarchical difficulty levels, OCR-aware placement to avoid trivial overlaps, and efficient implementation (3 hours for full dataset construction)
Strong reproducibility: detailed 18-page supplementary material, promise to release data-generation code enabling flexible dataset resampling, comprehensive implementation details

Clear architectural insights: Table 2 reveals that selective text use is primarily learned through language model reasoning rather than vision encoder modifications, contradicting prior vision-centric defenses
Well-written presentation with effective motivation: Figures 1 and 3 clearly communicate the problem and solution; practical relevance to autonomous vehicles and embodied AI systems
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: RIO-RT is straightforward balanced SFT on mixed object/text-attack data—a 'correct' training strategy rather than a novel defense mechanism; missing deeper analysis of why balanced training works

Scope constraints: evaluation limited to VQA tasks; no real-world deployment validation despite claims about autonomous vehicles; benchmark instantiated on TextVQA only, though pipeline is generalizable in principle

Generalization concerns: Table 4 shows domain-specific behavior (e.g., Llama-3.2-Vision IT-RT degrades RIO-Bench text reading but preserves external text-VQA performance), suggesting learned capability may not transfer broadly beyond scene text

Text-attack generation questions: LLM-based attack generation may introduce predictable patterns; OCR-based key text identification could fail on handwritten/stylized text; grid-based distance placement may not reflect naturalistic attack distributions

Modest improvement margins: RIO-RT gains over IT-RT on Text-Attack are often modest (8-9% for several models); raises questions about whether balanced training is minimal sufficient intervention or if more sophisticated approaches could yield better trade-offs

Missing error analysis and statistical testing: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; no detailed failure case analysis for RIO-RT; some percentage changes small enough to warrant formal significance testing
Ambiguous ground truth not discussed: some scenarios are genuinely ambiguous (e.g., misleading text in generic image descriptions); no treatment of annotation confidence or model disagreement cases

Benchmark scope: 21,953 training images is reasonable but modest; no analysis of whether performance plateaus or would benefit from larger data; generalization to non-VQA multimodal reasoning tasks (instruction following, visual reasoning) unexplored

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine misalignment between object-centric robustness evaluation and real-world multimodal requirements (e.g., autonomous vehicles reading traffic signs while ignoring inserted text)
Clever benchmark methodology: Same-scene counterfactual design with 2×2 factorial (object/text × clean/attack) effectively isolates read-or-ignore behavior while reducing dataset/scene confounds

Rigorous construction: Hierarchical negative sampling for MC questions, LLM-based attack generation, dual attack types (overlay + scene-coherent), strong human validation (95.5-97.5% desirable judgments, 90%+ IAA)
Novel metric: R-CLIP-M appropriately captures attack-aware robustness by penalizing consistency with attack words, addressing CLIP-M's blind spot
Comprehensive evaluation: 6 LVLMs, multiple question formats, attack difficulties, generalization analysis, scaling studies revealing frontier model vulnerabilities
Key empirical finding: Concrete demonstration that IT-RT improves Obj-Attack robustness (↑37%) while degrading Text-Clean by 20-50%, quantifying the robustness-text-reading trade-off
Interpretability: Attention analysis and LoRA ablations provide evidence that robustness comes from selective text disregard via language model reasoning, not global text suppression
Excellent documentation: Clear pipeline descriptions, reproducible hyperparameters, extensive implementation details in appendices
weaknesses: Limited task scope: Restricted to VQA; doesn't evaluate captioning, classification, or other LVLM capabilities. Only typographic attacks considered; no exploration of other adversarial perturbations or natural text variations

Benchmark scale and diversity: Built entirely on TextVQA (21,953 images) which is relatively modest. Object-centric questions synthetically generated (not natural). English-only; no multilingual coverage despite text being language-agnostic
Evaluation metric justification: R-CLIP-M choice of K=5 not empirically validated or justified. Sensitivity analysis missing. Text-VQA accuracy relies on fuzzy matching with potential instability

Defense evaluation is intentionally minimal: RIO-RT acknowledged as 'minimal reference baseline' without exploring alternative training objectives, data augmentation, vision encoder modifications, or architectural innovations. Doesn't explain why the trade-off exists fundamentally

Generalization concerns: Table 7 shows mixed transfer (IT-RT sometimes outperforms RIO-RT on Typo-D). LLaMA-3.2-Vision shows dramatic text-reading degradation on RIO-Bench but not on external datasets (Appendix F.2), suggesting domain-specific trade-off and questioning the benchmark's constraints

Statistical rigor absent: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Relative performance changes reported from sometimes small base rates. Single runs on some experiments not discussed. No analysis of which question types are fundamentally harder

Presentation: Figure 3 very dense and difficult to parse. Paper 33 pages long with critical details relegated to appendices. Design choices not justified in main text (e.g., why 16K training samples, K=5 for R-CLIP-M)
Incomplete ablations: R-CLIP-M design choices not validated (K sensitivity). LLM attack word generation quality variance not analyzed. RIO-RT data mixture ratios (4K+4K+8K) not explored

Limited analysis of inherent difficulty: Insufficient diagnosis of which scenarios are intrinsically hard. Attention visualization shown for only 2 cases. No analysis of whether models truly understand read-or-ignore or memorize patterns
Baseline novelty limited: RIO-RT is standard supervised fine-tuning with mixed data; not methodologically novel. No comparison with vision-focused defenses from [27, 37]. CoT baseline somewhat dated
